solver_candidate_counterexample: Parametric counterexample family: fix d = r = 1. For any proposed uniform support bound B, take the admissible odd integer n = 2B + 13. Then no Laurent polynomial C_{1,1,n}(X,q) supported in X-exponents [-B,B] can satisfy the required telescoping identities for k = 1,...,n-1.
solver_summary:
I believe the lemma is false.

Fix d = r = 1. Assume a uniform bound B exists. For any admissible odd n and any proposed witness C_n(X,q) = sum_{j=-B}^B c_j(q) X^j, the required identities for 1 <= k <= n-1 give

C_n(q^k,q) - R_k(q) C_n(q^{k+1},q) = 1,

with explicit ratio

R_k(q) = q^{-k-1} * (1-q^{3k+4})/(1-q^{3k+1}) * (1-q^{2k+1})^3 * (1-q^{k+1})/(1+q^{k+1}).

Equivalently, if

R(X,q) = q^{-1} X^{-1} (1-q^4 X^3)(1-q X^2)^3(1-qX) / ((1-qX^3)(1+qX)),
D(X,q) = (1-qX^3)(1+qX),
N(X,q) = q^{-1} X^{-1}(1-q^4 X^3)(1-qX^2)^3(1-qX),

then

P_n(X,q) := D(X,q)(C_n(X,q)-1) - N(X,q) C_n(qX,q)

satisfies P_n(q^k,q)=0 for k=1,...,n-1.

Because C_n has X-support in [-B,B], P_n has X-support in [-(B+1), B+9]. So X^{B+1} P_n is a polynomial in X of degree at most 2B+10 over Q(q). Taking n = 2B+13 (which is admissible), this polynomial has 2B+12 distinct roots X = q, q^2, ..., q^{2B+12}. Hence it must be the zero polynomial, so P_n(X,q)=0 identically.

Thus any such C_n would satisfy

D(X,q)(C_n(X,q)-1) = N(X,q) C_n(qX,q).

But no Laurent polynomial can satisfy this: if m is its minimal X-exponent and m<0, the left side has minimal exponent m while the right side has minimal exponent m-1; contradiction. Hence m>=0, so C_n is an ordinary polynomial of degree M. Then the left side has degree at most M+4, while the right side has degree exactly M+9 because N has leading term -q^7 X^9; contradiction.

Therefore for every proposed B, choosing d=r=1 and n=2B+13 gives a failure. So the lemma's uniform bounded-support certificate statement cannot be true.
vetter_reason: The submitted proof is empty, and the supplied counterexample family can be made rigorous. Fix d=r=1 and let B be any proposed uniform X-support bound. Take n=2B+13, which is admissible since n is odd. If C(X,q)=∑_{j=-B}^B c_j(q)X^j satisfied the telescoping identities for k=1,...,n-1, then with X=q^k those identities become 1 = C(X,q) - R(X,q) C(qX,q), where R(X,q)=q^{-1}X^{-1}(1-q^4X^3)(1-qX^2)^3(1-qX)/((1-qX^3)(1+qX)). After clearing denominators, F(X,q):=qX(1-qX^3)(1+qX)C(X,q) - (1-q^4X^3)(1-qX^2)^3(1-qX)C(qX,q) - qX(1-qX^3)(1+qX) is a Laurent polynomial in X with exponents contained in [-B,B+10], hence with at most 2B+11 X-monomials. But F(q^k,q)=0 for k=1,...,n-1=2B+12. Since the q^k are distinct over Q(q), the resulting Vandermonde system forces F(X,q)≡0. Now compare highest X-degree terms: if m is the largest exponent with c_m(q)≠0, then the second term contributes a nonzero X^{m+10} term q^{m+8}c_m(q)X^{m+10}, while the first term has X-degree at most m+5 and the final term has degree at most 5. So F cannot vanish identically. Contradiction. Therefore no such uniformly bounded-support certificate exists; the lemma statement is false.
